subsystems.name: Sensor mote
subsystems.role: the implant itself — a speck of silicon and crystal a few millimetres on a side that sits in tissue.

subsystems.name: Ultrasonic power and data link
subsystems.role: a patch or array outside the body sends sound pulses in and listens for the mote's reply.

subsystems.name: Energy harvester
subsystems.role: the crystal converts incoming ultrasound into the tiny amount of electricity the chip needs.

subsystems.name: Front-end circuit
subsystems.role: amplifies nerve signals, or drives a stimulation current, at microwatt power levels.

subsystems.name: Packaging
subsystems.role: keeps body fluid out of the electronics for years without stiffening the tissue around it.

subsystems.name: External decoding and control
subsystems.role: turns the reflected pulse stream into usable neural data or stimulation commands.

buildSteps.title: Design the chip
buildSteps.detail: Engineers lay out a CMOS circuit with only what is needed — amplifier, rectifier, a switch to reflect ultrasound back — because every transistor costs power and space.

buildSteps.title: Fabricate and thin the silicon
buildSteps.detail: The chip is made in a standard CMOS foundry, then ground down to a sliver thin enough to implant.

buildSteps.title: Bond the piezoelectric crystal
buildSteps.detail: A small piece of piezoelectric material is attached to the chip, becoming both its power source and its antenna.

buildSteps.title: Attach electrodes
buildSteps.detail: Fine leads are connected so the mote can sit on a nerve or in brain tissue and pick up or deliver charge.

buildSteps.title: Encapsulate
buildSteps.detail: Layers of thin-film coating are deposited to seal the device against salt water while keeping it flexible enough not to damage surrounding tissue.

buildSteps.title: Build the external transceiver
buildSteps.detail: A matched ultrasound array is assembled and calibrated to focus pulses on each mote and read its weak echo.

buildSteps.title: Bench test in fluid
buildSteps.detail: Motes are suspended in saline or gel, and the link is measured for range, power budget and data rate.

buildSteps.title: Implant in animals
buildSteps.detail: Devices are placed on peripheral nerves or in muscle in rodents and larger animals, then monitored for months to see how long they keep working.

buildSteps.title: Move to human use
buildSteps.detail: The remaining hurdles are surgical delivery, years-long reliability and regulatory approval for specific clinical uses.

prerequisites.why: the whole mote must run on microwatts harvested from sound, so the circuit has to be tiny and frugal.
they convert the external beam into power and encode the mote's signal in the reflection.
implants must survive years of warm, salty, moving tissue — the weakest link in the chain.
useful control signals must be extracted from noisy, drifting recordings.
thousands of separate motes need a practical way to be placed and, if needed, retrieved.

pathway.milestone: proof-of-concept motes recording nerve and muscle activity in animals, and versions that stimulate as well as sense
pathway.unlocks: evidence that ultrasound can power and query implants deep in tissue without wires.

pathway.milestone: chronic implants in larger animals with months-to-years lifetimes
pathway.unlocks: confidence that packaging and the acoustic link survive real biology.

pathway.milestone: first human clinical uses, likely on peripheral nerves for prosthetics or organ control
pathway.unlocks: a regulatory path and real patient data for a new class of interface.

pathway.milestone: large numbers of motes in the brain read and written by one external array
pathway.unlocks: high-bandwidth, fully wireless brain interfacing without a cable through the skull.
